title: A Comparative Analysis of Deep Learning Methods for Ghaf Tree Detection and Segmentation from UAV-based Images
authors: Hani Shanableh|Mohamed Barakat A. Gibril|Ahmed Mansour|Aditya Dixit|Rami Al-Ruzouq|Nezar Hammouri|Fouad Lamghari|Safa M. Ahmed|Ratiranjan Jena|Tilal Mohamed|Mohammed Abdulraheem Almarzouqi|Nedal Salem Alafayfeh|Simon Zerisenay Ghebremeskel
venue: ISPRS Annals of the Photogrammetry, Remote Sensing and Spatial Information Sciences
limitations: Wind-induced motion blur during UAV data acquisition causes loss of structural detail in Ghaf tree canopy, making Acacia trees appear similar to Ghaf trees due to fluffy, clouded, rounded appearance with grouped branches. Image tiling into 512×512 pixel patches results in significant context loss for trees positioned at tile edges, leading to missed detections or misclassifications. Intense reflections under certain lighting conditions cause some trees to appear similarly bright to Ghaf trees, complicating species discrimination. Difficulty in acquiring large, diverse ground-truth datasets across vast and heterogeneous areas where these trees are found. Potential errors introduced during tree count augmentation through image interpretation of RGB data alone. Including ambiguous cases in training data can reinforce misclassifications, complicating accurate discrimination between similar tree species. Limited to single modality (RGB only) which may miss important structural or spectral information available from multispectral or LiDAR sensors.

title: Evaluating deep learning methods applied to Landsat time series subsequences to detect and classify boreal forest disturbances events: The challenge of partial and progressive disturbances
authors: Pauline Perbet|Luc Guindon|Jean-François Côté|Martin Béland
limitations: The model struggles to classify partial disturbances with subtle spectral signatures at 30m resolution, such as partial windthrow and hemlock looper, often confusing them with healthy forest. The accuracy of dating disturbances is affected by cloud/shadow cover in the Landsat composites. The model cannot detect multiple disturbances within the same year (e.g., fire followed by salvage logging).

title: Fine-grained individual tree crown segmentation based on high-resolution images
authors: Yinrui Wang|Xintong Dou|Xinlian Liang
venue: The International Archives of the Photogrammetry, Remote Sensing and Spatial Information Sciences, Volume XLVIII-G-2025, ISPRS Geospatial Week 2025
limitations: Authors acknowledge multiple limitations: (1) Generalization challenges - 'the generalization of the SOTA networks is required to be improved' with dramatic performance drops on unseen datasets (4.07% AP50 on Dataset 11); (2) Transferability issues - 'The low performance in Dataset 10 and 11 represent the improvement potential of the transferability'; (3) Strong dependency on data characteristics - resolution, image quality, forest type, and canopy density significantly impact performance; (4) SAM foundation model inadequacy - severe miss-segmentation and under-segmentation in zero-shot mode; (5) Training scheme sensitivity - excessive training epochs damage performance, requiring careful early-stopping; (6) Geographic bias - models trained predominantly on Northern Hemisphere data fail to generalize to Australian savanna woodland.

title: Instance Segmentation of LiDAR Data with Vision Transformer Model in Support Inundation Mapping under Forest Canopy Environment
authors: Jian Yang|Lamiae El Mendili|Yasmin Khayer|Steven McArdle|Leila Hashemi Beni
limitations: Authors acknowledge several limitations: (1) The Mask2Former model requires large amounts of training data to achieve good performance, which may not be available or feasible for some regions or scenarios; (2) Data quality and variety is crucial to improve model robustness; (3) The model may benefit from incorporating auxiliary information such as multispectral imagery to enhance discriminative power; (4) Constrained availability and quality of crown samples, as well as dense forest canopies, curtail the full potential of Mask2Former-based ITC segmentation; (5) The lower detection rate (87%) compared to watershed baseline (100%) is attributed to the pre-processing step that removes non-tree objects, suggesting deep learning models may be more robust without pre-cleaning but requires further testing.

title: EarthDial: Turning Multi-sensory Earth Observations to Interactive Dialogues
authors: Sagar Soni|Akshay Dudhane|Hiyam Debary|Mustansar Fiaz|Muhammad Akhtar Munir|Muhammad Sohail Danish|Paolo Fraccaro|Campbell D Watson|Levente J Klein|Fahad Shahbaz Khan|Salman Khan
venue: CVPR (Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition)
limitations: Authors acknowledge: (1) model is relatively lightweight (4B parameters) compared to larger VLMs but still requires significant computational resources (4x A100 80GB GPUs for training), (2) adaptive high-resolution processing limited to 40 tiles during inference which may constrain very high-resolution imagery processing, (3) data fusion module processes 3 channels at a time which may not be optimal for all multi-spectral configurations, (4) temporal sequence analysis limited to specific bi-temporal and multi-temporal formats, (5) vision encoder frozen after Stage 1 which may limit fine-grained visual adaptation to new domains, (6) evaluation focused on existing benchmarks without extensive cross-biome transfer testing

title: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Individual Tree Crown Detection and Species Classification Using UAV-Acquired Imagery
authors: Jiuyu Zhang|Fan Lei|Xijian Fan
limitations: Model trained on natural images (Grounding-DINO) shows poor zero-shot performance (AP50=2.4) on UAV remote sensing imagery, requiring fine-tuning for effective adaptation. Direct application struggles to accurately localize trees in UAV images with multiple species. Future research will focus on expanding the method to address a broader range of species present in images (currently limited to 3 species). Dataset characterized by relatively small number of image samples (300 images), which tests transferability to limited-data scenarios.

title: Assessing the Generalization Capacity of Convolutional Neural Networks and Vision Transformers for Deforestation Detection in Tropical Biomes
authors: Pedro J. Soto Vega|Daliana Lobo Torres|Gustavo X. Andrade-Miranda|Gilson A. O. P. da Costa|Raul Queiroz Feitosa
venue: ISPRS Archives of the Photogrammetry, Remote Sensing and Spatial Information Sciences
limitations: Authors acknowledge that lower accuracy of transformer-based model in cross-domain scenarios may be influenced by various problems, such as overfitting. The study considers further investigation needed with additional architectures (transformer, convolutional and hybrid) and a wider range of domains and applications. Authors note the complexity of forested and deforested regions varies across domains (forest complexity lowest in PA and highest in MA, deforestation complexity opposite), affecting model transferability. Limited to three domains within Brazilian tropical biomes. Requires further research to confirm findings.

title: Sustainable Forestry: AI-Driven Forest Health Diagnostics using Swin Transformer
authors: Shaik Rasheeda Begum|Vaibhav Mishra|Devmalaya Saha
venue: 2025 International Conference on Advances in Modern Age Technologies for Health and Engineering Science (AMATHE)
limitations: Authors acknowledge that model performance relies on the quality and diversity of training data. Environmental factors like variable lighting and dense canopy cover may impact detection accuracy. The study suggests that incorporating thermal and multispectral data could improve performance under challenging conditions. The model requires high-resolution data for accurate detection. Applicability is limited under low visibility or high canopy density conditions. The study also notes the need for real-time monitoring capabilities and predictive modeling to correlate tree health with fire risk indicators.

title: More appropriate DenseNetBL classifier for small sample tree species classification using UAV-based RGB imagery
authors: Ni Wang|Tao Pu|Yali Zhang|Yuchan Liu|Zeyu Zhang
limitations: Authors acknowledge: (1) Small sample size limits generalization - 'manually creating tree species dataset is challenging due to limited images and range'; (2) SLIC segmentation struggles with 'uneven tree crown sizes' and 'complex forest environment'; (3) Vision Transformer failed to converge in 30 epochs on small data; (4) Deep transformers exhibit 'underfitting on small sample datasets due to complex structure and multiple hyperparameters'; (5) Geographic limitation - only one study site with two typical forests; (6) Species imbalance - Osmanthus fragrans severely underrepresented (32 training samples) leading to poor classification (CA=0.057 for DenseNet33BL); (7) Need for 'semi-supervised algorithm with multiple classifiers' and 'multi-temporal high spatial resolution images' for future improvement.

title: DOFA-CLIP: Multimodal Vision–Language Foundation Models for Earth Observation
authors: Zhitong Xiong|Yi Wang|Weikang Yu|Adam J Stewart|Jie Zhao|Nils Lehmann|Thomas Dujardin|Zhenghang Yuan|Pedram Ghamisi|Xiao Xiang Zhu
limitations: 1) Performance on multispectral 5-band inputs decreases compared to RGB due to significantly less multispectral training data in GeoLangBind-2M; 2) Zero-shot multi-label classification on complex datasets (m-bigearthnet) shows moderate performance (F1: 23.69%); 3) Fine-grained attribute classification tasks (roof smoothness) remain challenging (26.00% accuracy with ViT-L-384); 4) Weight merging ratios require manual linear search optimization rather than automatic determination; 5) Model requires large GPU memory (40-80GB) for training; 6) Current approach uses simple linear weight merging rather than more sophisticated merging methods; 7) Text descriptions for some modalities generated synthetically using Pixtral-12B, which may introduce bias or quality variations.

title: Tree-GPT: Modular Large Language Model Expert System for Forest Remote Sensing Image Understanding and Interactive Analysis
authors: S. Q. Du|S.J. Tang|W. X. Wang|X. M. Li|R. Z. Guo
limitations: Authors acknowledge: (1) SAM's segmentation quality highly sensitive to input prompts, requiring custom prompt generation framework, (2) SAM generates many redundant masks without semantic information, necessitating bipartite graph matching post-processing, (3) Segmentation granularity not controllable in SAM without prior knowledge, (4) System requires high-resolution data (<0.5m implied by 0.025m test data) for accurate tree detection and segmentation, (5) LLMs exhibit 'hallucination' generating inaccurate professional knowledge without domain-specific fine-tuning, requiring Domain Knowledge Base retrieval, (6) Interactive visualization may require 'multiple manual guidance to achieve the best visualization effect' rather than correct results in first round, (7) Foundation models' computational costs not analyzed - no discussion of inference time or resource requirements for real-time forestry applications.

title: Seasonal Forest Disturbance Detection Using Sentinel-1 SAR & Sentinel-2 Optical Timeseries Data and Transformers
authors: Adugna Mullissa|Johannes Reiche|Sassan Saatchi
venue: IGARSS 2023 - IEEE International Geoscience and Remote Sensing Symposium
limitations: Authors acknowledge: (1) Limited dataset size used in experiments poses challenges to model efficacy, (2) Missing data from Sentinel-2 timeseries due to cloud cover and shadows, (3) Computational complexity cost of the Transformer architecture, (4) Need to improve generalization capability through more diverse training datasets, (5) Future work needed to address missing data through gap estimation and filling approaches, (6) Need to explore different fusion approaches to improve robustness

title: SSMM-DS: A semantic segmentation model for mangroves based on Deeplabv3+ with swin transformer
authors: Zhenhua Wang|Jinlong Yang|Chuansheng Dong|Xi Zhang|Congqin Yi|Jiuhu Sun
limitations: Authors acknowledge: (1) Computational efficiency limitations hindering large-scale deployment and real-time monitoring; (2) Scarcity of mangrove samples and spectral similarity with other vegetation limiting generalization; (3) Need for lightweight network design, model compression, and hardware-aware optimization for UAV/edge deployment; (4) Sample imbalance requiring advanced learning strategies (active learning, semi-supervised, transfer learning); (5) Model interpretability needed to understand decision-making and guide optimization; (6) Requirement for multi-source data fusion (Sentinel, Gaofen, UAV) for comprehensive monitoring; (7) Need for intelligent monitoring platform enabling real-time tracking and early warning of mangrove changes.

title: Multi-modal Uncertainty Robust Tree Cover Segmentation For High-Resolution Remote Sensing Images
authors: Yuanyuan Gui|Wei Li|Yinjian Wang|Xiang-Gen Xia|Mauro Marty|Christian Ginzler|Zuyuan Wang
limitations: Authors acknowledge: (1) Temporal mismatch between multi-modal acquisitions (days to years apart) introduces significant aleatoric uncertainty, particularly pronounced in high-resolution imagery; (2) Frequent vegetation changes including pruning, harvesting, or seasonal defoliation may reduce segmentation accuracy; (3) GPU memory constraints limit batch size to 5 on 24GB GPU; (4) Datasets are custom and not publicly available, limiting reproducibility; (5) Geographic bias - only tested on European (Switzerland) and Asian (China) urban/temperate environments; (6) Model requires paired multi-modal data which may not always be available in operational settings.

title: Benchmarking Individual Tree Mapping with Sub-meter Imagery
authors: Dimitri Gominski|Ankit Kariryaa|Martin Brandt|Christian Igel|Sizhuo Li|Maurice Mugabowindekwe|Rasmus Fensholt
venue: arXiv preprint (submitted to ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing)
limitations: Authors acknowledge that 'only overstory trees can be identified from an aerial perspective' with bias towards large trees (13% for large trees, 47% bias if considering all woody plants from field data). 'Even expert annotators can make errors' with 35.2% disagreement rate between two annotators in dense forests. Authors note the 'high annotation cost of segmentation' and that 'trees represent challenging variations for mapping due to differences in size, shapes and context related to species and environmental conditions.' Key limitation: 'the core of the problem lies in separating trees' through instance segmentation rather than improving feature extraction. Authors emphasize need for 'adding robustness to label noise, or correcting labels, rather than developing new models and architectures.' Transformer architectures show no clear advantage over CNNs despite higher parameter counts and computational costs.

title: A Vision Transformer Model for Convolution-Free Multilabel Classification of Satellite Imagery in Deforestation Monitoring
authors: Maria Kaselimi|Athanasios Voulodimos|Ioannis Daskalopoulos|Nikolaos Doulamis|Anastasios Doulamis
venue: IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems
limitations: Authors acknowledge that computational complexity during training is notably higher than ResNet (37% greater), though comparable during inference. The model was only evaluated on Amazon basin data, limiting conclusions about generalization to other tropical or non-tropical forests. The approach requires high-quality satellite imagery with appropriate resolution. The challenge of heterogeneous deforestation drivers within images and rapid landscape evolution makes automation difficult. The dataset's inherent imbalance (rare deforestation events vs large forestry areas) poses challenges for standard deep learning approaches, though ForestViT addresses this better than CNNs.

title: SatelliteCalculator: A Multi-Task Vision Foundation Model for Quantitative Remote Sensing Inversion
authors: Zhenyu Yu|Mohd. Yamani Idna Idris|Pei Wang
limitations: Authors acknowledge: (1) Structural variables (AGB, CS) show significantly larger prediction errors (AGB RMSE: 26.04 t/ha, CS RMSE: 21.84 Mg/ha) compared to spectral indices (NDVI RMSE: 0.22) due to dependence on complex environmental and regional factors beyond spectral reflectance alone, (2) Performance degrades in heterogeneous regions such as forest edges and bare land areas for biomass estimation tasks, (3) Model trained only on French temperate forests (Open-Canopy dataset) with no cross-biome or cross-environment validation reported, limiting assessment of geographic generalization, (4) Empirical coefficients for AGB and CS estimation are region-specific and may require recalibration for different forest types or geographic areas, (5) Foundation model approach inherits spectral domain shift challenges when transferring ImageNet pretraining to remote sensing despite successful adaptation.

title: Novel Single Tree Detection by Transformers Using UAV-based Multispectral Imagery
authors: S. Dersch|A. Schöttl|P. Krzystek|M. Heurich
venue: The International Archives of the Photogrammetry, Remote Sensing and Spatial Information Sciences, XXIV ISPRS Congress
limitations: DETR struggles with small tree detection (detected only 1 of 7 small coniferous trees vs YOLOv4's 4 of 7), attributed to transformers' known difficulty with small objects compared to methods using higher resolution feature maps. Both DETR and YOLOv4 exhibit over-segmentation in deciduous areas, particularly for large tree crowns (15m diameter crowns split into multiple detections). This over-segmentation is attributed to training data containing mainly medium-sized trees. The limited amount of training data (1390 trees) necessitated use of pre-trained COCO model. DETR converges slower than comparable object detection methods. Performance varies significantly by forest type (71-86% F1-score range). Future work needed: (i) integration of multispectral channels (NIR, NDVI, NDRE), (ii) fusion with LiDAR-based metrics (DSM, intensity, penetration rate), (iii) extension to tree crown segmentation beyond detection.

title: Integrating Hyperspectral Images and LiDAR Data Using Vision Transformers for Enhanced Vegetation Classification
authors: Xingquan Shu|Limin Ma|Fengqin Chang
limitations: Authors acknowledge: (1) Model performance may be constrained by availability and diversity of training data - expanding dataset to include more varied environmental conditions and plant species would improve robustness; (2) Integration of multiple data types (HSI and LiDAR) with advanced transformers and involution increases model complexity, presenting challenges for computational cost and real-time deployment in large-scale monitoring systems; (3) Standard ViT architectures are computationally intensive, limiting practical applicability for UAV-based real-time monitoring; (4) ViTs require extensive labeled training datasets, limiting applicability in ecological studies where labeled samples are scarce; (5) Trade-off exists between efficiency and classification accuracy in lightweight transformer models

title: Spectral–Spatial transformer-based semantic segmentation for large-scale mapping of individual date palm trees using very high-resolution satellite data
authors: Rami Al-Ruzouq|Mohamed Barakat A. Gibril|Abdallah Shanableh|Jan Bolcek|Fouad Lamghari|Nezar Atalla Hammour|Ali El-Keblawy|Ratiranjan Jena
limitations: Authors acknowledge: (1) Difficulty delineating smaller date palm trees due to limited spatial resolution (1.24m GSD) of satellite data; (2) Manual annotation is labor-intensive and time-consuming, requiring aid from aerial/UAV data; (3) Performance varies with acquisition dates, illumination conditions, and surrounding environments; (4) UperNet-ViT did not effectively utilize spectral information, resulting in oversegmentation and misclassification; (5) Need for further exploration of handcrafted spectral indices' influence on ViT performance; (6) Requirement for self-supervised or semi-supervised techniques to expedite ground-truth data preparation; (7) Potential benefit from super-resolution deep learning to enhance spatial resolution and improve detection of small trees in heterogeneous areas

title: Fusing SENTINEL-1 AND SENTINEL-2 images with transformer-based network for deforestation detection in the Brazilian Amazon under diverse cloud conditions
authors: F. Ferrari|M. P. Ferreira|R. Q. Feitosa
venue: ISPRS Annals of the Photogrammetry, Remote Sensing and Spatial Information Sciences
limitations: Authors acknowledge that TRA-OPT's behavior in cloudy conditions (higher precision but lower recall) requires further investigation. The spatial resolution difference between PRODES Landsat-based labels (30m) and Sentinel imagery (10m) required applying a 3-pixel buffer to deforestation polygons. The study was limited to a single geographic region (~12,500 km²) in the Brazilian Amazon without cross-region validation. Authors note that 'investigations using other architectures are required to validate these findings' and suggest 'further investigations into the role of the information source (optical and SAR) in the fusion models may clarify its behavior in diverse cloud conditions.' The reliance on PRODES polygons limits detection to clear-cutting deforestation ≥6.25 hectares.

title: FoMo: Multi-Modal, Multi-Scale and Multi-Task Remote Sensing Foundation Models for Forest Monitoring
authors: Nikolaos Ioannis Bountos|Arthur Ouaknine|Ioannis Papoutsis|David Rolnick
limitations: Authors acknowledge: (1) FoMo-Net does not consistently outperform specialized supervised models, particularly with abundant labeled data; (2) Evaluating flexible foundation models requires methods beyond performance metrics to assess modality recognition and scale understanding; (3) Independent band tokenization creates computational bottleneck - memory requirements and quadratic attention complexity pose scalability challenges; (4) Optimization is a priority given these constraints; (5) Current pre-training limited to 64×64 patches and max 4 spectral bands for efficiency; (6) Point cloud data excluded due to need for specialized processing; (7) Model capacity (12-layer ViT) may be insufficient for digesting diverse global information; (8) Lack of built-in hierarchical features in ViT for dense prediction; (9) Authors note combining FoMo-Net with supervised pre-training (like PolyNet) could prove valuable but remains unexplored; (10) TalloS dataset challenges: extreme class imbalance with 1000+ tree genera, many rare species limited to specific locations, tree species occurrence maps as biological prior could help but not yet incorporated

title: Transformer-Based Semantic Segmentation of Japanese Knotweed in High-Resolution UAV Imagery Using Twins-SVT
authors: Sruthi Keerthi Valicharla|Roghaiyeh Karimzadeh|Xin Li|Yong-Lak Park
limitations: Manual annotation required considerable effort due to difficulty visually differentiating knotweed from surrounding vegetation, especially under dense or overlapping canopy conditions. Variability in vegetation height and shadowing complicated accurate boundary delineation. Aerial surveys conducted only during summer, limiting model applicability to vegetative and flowering stages of Japanese knotweed. Need for field-level validation to assess generalizability across different ecological regions, vegetation types, and UAV platforms. Incorporating temporal data from multi-season surveys may enhance ability to monitor phenological variations. Need to explore computational efficiency improvements including model compression and deployment optimizations. Need to test robustness for fragmented habitats (urban edges, mixed agriculture). Future work should investigate domain adaptation and transfer learning for varying environmental conditions.

title: A Comprehensive Evaluation of Monocular Depth Estimation Methods in Low-Altitude Forest Environment
authors: Jiwen Jia|Junhua Kang|Lin Chen|Xiang Gao|Borui Zhang|Guijun Yang
limitations: This is an evaluation paper assessing existing models. Key challenges identified: (1) CNN-based models struggle with depth discontinuities in dense forest environments, producing over-smooth predictions; (2) Transformer models, while superior, require large-scale diverse training data for robust generalization; (3) Models trained on limited domains (e.g., indoor scenes) fail to transfer to forest environments; (4) Depth estimation accuracy degrades with increasing distance from camera; (5) Real-world forest complexity (lighting, occlusions, texture) exceeds synthetic dataset challenges; (6) Shaded/dimly lit regions remain challenging even for best models; (7) Computational requirements (RTX 4090 GPU needed) limit deployment; (8) Ground-truth depth from RGB-D cameras in real forests is poor quality, limiting validation.

title: UAV4TREE: DEEP LEARNING-BASED SYSTEM FOR AUTOMATIC CLASSIFICATION OF TREE SPECIES USING RGB OPTICAL IMAGES OBTAINED BY AN UNMANNED AERIAL VEHICLE
authors: Roberto Pierdicca|Lindo Nepi|Adriano Mancini|Eva Savina Malinverni|Mattia Balestra
venue: ISPRS Annals of the Photogrammetry, Remote Sensing and Spatial Information Sciences
limitations: Authors acknowledge multiple limitations: 1) Significant domain shift between ground-level training images and aerial UAV test images causing performance degradation; 2) Limited dataset size initially (2,690 training images) affecting model performance; 3) Weather conditions, camera calibration, image resolution, flight path/altitude variations impact UAV RGB image quality and accuracy; 4) Processing challenges with obstructions or lighting changes during UAV flights; 5) Manual annotation burden for large training datasets; 6) Class imbalance and noise in test dataset, particularly for Quercus pubescens; 7) Seasonal phenological variations in tree crown appearance reducing classification accuracy; 8) Difficulty manually annotating UAV images where multiple species present in same frame; 9) Requires extensive augmentation and fine-tuning to achieve acceptable generalization from ground to aerial views; 10) Some models (ResNet, InceptionV3) showed overfitting despite high validation accuracy; 11) SR-GAN processing adds computational overhead but necessary for some models to achieve acceptable performance on UAV imagery.

title: Vision Transformers, a new approach for high-resolution and large-scale mapping of canopy heights
authors: Ibrahim Fayad|Philippe Ciais|Martin Schwartz|Jean-Pierre Wigneron|Nicolas Baghdadi|Aurélien de Truchis|Alexandre d'Aspremont|Frederic Frappart|Sassan Saatchi|Agnes Pellissier-Tanon|Hassan Bazzi
limitations: Authors acknowledge: (1) GEDI calibration data limitations - 4m pulse width limits sensitivity to vegetation <4m, geolocation errors up to 10m especially in sparse areas, saturation/underestimation in very dense forests, coverage beam vs full power beam quality differences. (2) Minimum height estimates ~2.5-3m over bare soil/water due to GEDI limitations. (3) All models underestimate very tall trees >40m due to limited training samples and GEDI sensor saturation. (4) 15-month mosaicking approach masks temporal events (fires, logging) occurring near end of period. (5) ConvNet models (α-2MDU) require post-processing to mask urban areas, while this is unnecessary for Hy-TeC. (6) Higher computational/memory requirements of transformers may limit adoption. (7) Height map validation limited by ALS coverage (10km²) and lack of ground truth over full Ghana extent.

title: Monitoring Forest Changes With Foundation Models and Sentinel-2 Time Series
authors: Jakub Sadel|Lukasz Tulczyjew|Agata M. Wijata|Mateusz Przeliorz|Jakub Nalepa
venue: IEEE Geoscience and Remote Sensing Letters
limitations: Authors acknowledge: (1) Relatively low segmentation results across all models attributed to extremely high heterogeneity of test composite images and cloud contamination (26% minor occlusions, 5% major quality issues); (2) Monthly composite images suffer from cloud artifacts that directly affect learned models as no cloud detection/removal preprocessing was performed; (3) DynamicEarthNet agriculture class contains vegetation pixels similar to forest class, causing confusion; (4) TransUNet models struggled to optimize without pre-trained weights for the different input channel characteristics; (5) Cloudy Sentinel-2 images would be annotated as 'useless' in practical scenarios and should be handled by on-board smart compression/selection techniques; (6) Appropriately handling contaminated images in training and inference stages needs further research; (7) Some test AOIs (3, 7, 8) notably more challenging with accuracy <60%; (8) Models tend to over-report deforestation, requiring manual verification of detected changes.

title: ForestFormer3D: A Unified Framework for End-to-End Segmentation of Forest LiDAR 3D Point Clouds
authors: Binbin Xiang|Maciej Wielgosz|Stefano Puliti|Kamil Král|Martin Krůček|Azim Missarov|Rasmus Astrup
limitations: Authors acknowledge: (1) Small trees occasionally missed, particularly in dense multi-layered forests. (2) Heavily inclined small trees near ground pose significant challenge for all methods, leading to missed detections, over-segmentation, or incorrect assignment to neighboring trees - identified as 'open problem for future research'. (3) Performance degrades significantly in extremely sparse point clouds (<100 pts/m²), and multi-density training augmentation provides only partial mitigation without solving the fundamental challenge. (4) Semantic segmentation mIoU slightly lower than CNN baseline ForAINetV2 (-1.3 pp on test split, -0.5 pp on validation) due to unified architecture prioritizing instance-level distinctions through shared representation learning. (5) GPU memory constraints limited exploration of larger input radii and more query points which could potentially improve performance further. (6) Cylinder cropping can split individual trees, requiring boundary masking mitigation strategy

title: Leveraging Prompt-Based Segmentation Models and Large Dataset to Improve Detection of Trees
authors: Vincent Grondin|Philippe Massicotte|Mohamed Gaha|François Pomerleau|Philippe Giguère
limitations: Authors acknowledge: 1) SAM can wrongly associate background branches to trees, causing bounding boxes to cover larger areas that hurt performance if labels don't include branches; 2) The released dataset images are sourced from Flickr with varying licenses, so only URL links will be provided (not self-contained); 3) Some downloaded images 'may not necessarily feature trees, rendering them irrelevant for tree detection purposes' as no human verification was performed post-download; 4) Performance gains from SAM pseudo-labels are minimal on 'easy' datasets with straight tree trunks (CANATREE100); 5) Running three models simultaneously (burn-in, SAM, finetuning) would be GPU memory intensive, limiting deployment options; 6) Future improvement needed: 'finetune HQ-SAM on forest images so it learns to output correctly segmented trees even with noisy prompt inputs'.

title: TransU-Net++: Rethinking attention gated TransU-Net for deforestation mapping
authors: Ali Jamali|Swalpa Kumar Roy|Jonathan Li|Pedram Ghamisi
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
limitations: Authors acknowledge that ViTs face several challenges in remote sensing: (1) significant complexity that increases computation costs, and (2) need for much higher reference data than CNNs. The paper notes that while the developed TransU-Net++ model was evaluated for deforestation mapping, the generalized architecture could be applied to other computer vision tasks (remote sensing segmentation, medical image segmentation, smoke semantic segmentation). Future work should evaluate the architecture in medical image segmentation domain. The paper emphasizes that consistent visual and statistical performance across multiple datasets is more important than slight advantages in specific statistical indices on individual datasets

title: Transformer-based Instance Segmentation with Multi-Scale Spectrum-Averaging Blend Queries
authors: Lirong Zhu|Chih-Wei Lin|Ye Lin
venue: 9th International Symposium on Computer and Information Processing Technology (ISCIPT)
limitations: Authors acknowledge that initial queries being randomly generated can impact performance. Additionally, positional queries experience information lag because they are updated only during backpropagation rather than being directly mapped, which prevents the model from promptly updating position information based on current input.

title: Vision Transformer-Based Unhealthy Tree Crown Detection in Mixed Northeastern US Forests and Evaluation of Annotation Uncertainty
authors: Durga Joshi|Chandi Witharana
limitations: Authors acknowledge multiple significant limitations: (1) Dense canopy with significant crown occlusion made distinguishing individual trees difficult, particularly between healthy and unhealthy trees with similar spectral signatures; (2) Data acquired during early fall introduced additional noise as spectral reflectance of unhealthy trees might be similar to senescent-colored foliage, leading to segmentation errors; (3) Manual annotation in dense and visually complex scenes was time-consuming and susceptible to human bias, with substantial inter-annotator variability (IoU scores ranging from 0.37 to 0.70 among 9 annotators); (4) The 60cm spatial resolution might be insufficient to resolve details within dense canopy, potentially leading to spectral mixing and reduced accuracy; (5) Annotation scale choice (1:300) might not capture finer details crucial for precise segmentation in occluded areas; (6) Model exhibited boundary extent uncertainty, with tendency to overestimate larger UTC areas; (7) Annotation uncertainty analysis revealed IoU could fluctuate between 14.81% to 57.41% and F1-scores from 8.57% to 47.14% depending on annotation strategy (intersection vs union vs median consensus), demonstrating significant sensitivity to annotation inconsistencies; (8) Occluded and merged canopies posed difficulties in accurate individual crown delineation, often resulting in multiple UTCs being annotated as single crowns; (9) Limited to single geographic region (Connecticut) and single season (early fall), limiting generalizability claims.

title: Towards complete tree crown delineation by instance segmentation with Mask R–CNN and DETR using UAV-based multispectral imagery and lidar data
authors: S. Dersch|A. Schöttl|P. Krzystek|M. Heurich
venue: ISPRS Open Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
limitations: Both instance segmentation methods only detect trees visible in the upper canopy, missing regeneration and smaller trees in lower forest layers. Potential solutions require 3D instance segmentation methods with sufficient LiDAR point density in lower layers. Training process requires considerably large forest area (~1000-1500 trees of different species, composition and sizes) to adequately train the network, which may exceed benefit for small drone-captured areas without special permission. LiDAR-derived stem information (P_DENSE) insufficient for deciduous trees where dense canopy prevents laser penetration. Under-segmentation and over-segmentation still occur, particularly for closely spaced trees and trees with complex crown shapes. Small trees (<15m²) difficult to detect. Study does not address transferability of neural networks to other forest structures. Authors note need for more general network models applicable to various forest areas with different structures.

title: Estimating Urban Forests Biomass with LiDAR by Using Deep Learning Foundation Models
authors: Hanzhang Liu|Chao Mou|Jiateng Yuan|Zhibo Chen|Liheng Zhong|Xiaohui Cui
limitations: Authors acknowledge: (1) Model performance may be limited in cities with complex meteorological conditions where LiDAR image quality is low; (2) In urban areas prone to natural disasters, changes in spatial layout may deviate from socio-economic development patterns, challenging consistent estimation; (3) High-quality LiDAR data required - may struggle with missing or incomplete data; (4) Higher computational cost at inference time due to large foundation model parameters, though training cost is dramatically reduced; (5) SAM occasionally struggles with missing trees, inaccurate height parameters, and indistinct canopy boundaries in very dense vegetation; (6) Model may require reducing frozen layers (higher training cost) for areas with complex meteorological conditions; (7) Need more temporal data collection in areas with irregular spatial layout changes to improve adaptation.

title: Bringing SAM to new heights: Leveraging elevation data for tree crown segmentation from drone imagery
authors: Mélisande Teng|Arthur Ouaknine|Etienne Laliberté|Yoshua Bengio|David Rolnick|Hugo Larochelle
limitations: Authors acknowledge: (1) SAM out-of-the-box fails to separate overlapping crowns, generates false positives on background/tiny plants, misses trees in areas with tall herbaceous vegetation; (2) Prompting SAM with trained detector outputs degrades rather than improves performance; (3) RSPrompter and BalSAM demonstrate higher variance than baseline methods; (4) Classification challenges with long-tailed training data not fully addressed (beyond weighted/hierarchical loss experiments); (5) DSM benefit highly dependent on canopy structural complexity - greatest for plantations with well-separated trees, minimal for dense temperate forests where individual trees barely stand out in DSM; (6) BCI dataset has missing annotations from undetected crowns requiring manual masking; (7) DSM for BCI only available at coarse 1m-height resolution; (8) Potential dual-use risks (models trained to identify species targeted in illegal logging); (9) Methods require high-resolution drone imagery (<5cm resolution) for effective performance; (10) Computational requirements substantial (48-80GB GPU memory, 1-5 days training)

title: WetMapFormer: A unified deep CNN and vision transformer for complex wetland mapping
authors: Ali Jamali|Swalpa Kumar Roy|Pedram Ghamisi
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
limitations: Authors acknowledge: (1) Higher computation costs due to LWA concepts compared to pure CNN models, though substantially lower than vanilla ViTs; (2) By decreasing number of LWA blocks, computational cost can be reduced but may impact performance; (3) Slightly lower performance for some site-specific classes compared to ViT/Swin with larger receptive fields (e.g., bog classification in York county: ViT 0.99 vs WetMapFormer 0.98 F-1); (4) Increasing receptive field size would capture larger context but significantly increase computational cost for large-scale mapping; (5) Vision transformer-based algorithms generally incur significantly higher computational costs than CNN-based classifiers in terms of hardware and running time; (6) Wetlands inherently complex with lack of defined boundaries, fuzzy transitions to other land cover classes; (7) High degree of similarity between some wetland species (bog and fen have similar spectral reflectance); (8) Same wetland species can have different spectral characteristics across different spatial and temporal conditions due to extreme dynamics; (9) Water found underneath surface, within canopy, or in soil makes distinguishing backscattering/spectral signatures challenging; (10) Gathering training samples for remote sensing applications typically costly; (11) Future work needed to decrease computational cost in terms of running time and hardware requirements.

title: VibrantVS: A High-Resolution Vision Transformer for Forest Canopy Height Estimation
authors: Tony Chang|Kiarie Ndegwa|Andreas Gros|Vincent A. Landau|Luke J. Zachmann|Bogdan State|Mitchell A. Gritts|Colton W. Miller|Nathan E. Rutenbeck|Scott Conway|Guy Bayes
limitations: Authors acknowledge multiple limitations: (1) Underestimation of very tall trees (>50m) due to training data imbalance - such trees represent <0.5% of training data and occur only in few ecoregions; (2) All models perform worse in high-altitude areas and steep slopes, potentially from training data imbalance as sampling map (Figure 1) shows concentration in lower elevations; (3) Training/test data cover only a small fraction of western US area and environmental/ecological diversity, limiting generalization claims; (4) Overestimation in lowest height bin (2-5m) because tree crown spatial footprint appears larger in NAIP than lidar, requiring block-level rather than pixel-level metrics to address; (5) All four models including VibrantVS truncate tree heights above 50m (Figure 6, Figure 8); (6) Temporal mismatch between NAIP imagery and lidar acquisition dates for baseline models (though VibrantVS maintains <1 year alignment); (7) Future improvements needed: integrate topography data for steep slopes/high altitude, expand to central/eastern US and lower vegetation heights (<2m), increase sampling of tall tree species for better representation.

title: Efficient Large-scale Mapping of Acacia Tortilis Trees Using UAV-based Images and Transformer-based Semantic Segmentation Architectures
authors: Mohamed Barakat A. Gibril|Abdallah Shanableh|Rami Al-Ruzouq|Nezar Hammouri|Fouad Lamghari|Safa M. Ahmed|Ahmed Mansour|Ratiranjan Jena|Hani Shanableh|Mohammed Abdulraheem Almarzouqi|Nedal Salem Alafayfeh|Simon Zerisenay Ghebremeskel
venue: ISPRS Annals of the Photogrammetry, Remote Sensing and Spatial Information Sciences (ISPRS Geospatial Week 2025, Dubai, UAE)
limitations: Longer training time for the proposed DaViT backbone; occasional misclassification with Prosopis juliflora; reduced detectability in mountainous backgrounds where crowns blend into substrate; dataset expansion relied partly on manual image interpretation/Google Street View which may introduce minor label noise; future work suggested on expanding geographic coverage for better generalizability and exploring semi-supervised approaches.

title: Bridging Classical and Modern Computer Vision: PerceptiveNet for Tree Crown Semantic Segmentation
authors: Georgios Voulgaris
limitations: Authors acknowledge that PerceptiveNeTr (hybrid CNN-Transformer model) shows lower performance metrics compared to pure CNN PerceptiveNet, indicating need for further development through integration of advanced transformer models such as Hierarchical Vision Transformer or pre-trained models. Paper focuses on architectural innovations rather than computational efficiency, with no reported metrics on parameter count or inference time which limits assessment of practical deployment feasibility. Dense forests present unique challenges including variable lighting conditions and shadows, complex backgrounds with overlapping canopies, scale variations from different UAV heights, and subtle spectral differences between species.

title: Deep convolutional neural networks and Swin transformer-based frameworks for individual date palm tree detection and mapping from large-scale UAV images
authors: Mohamed Barakat A. Gibril|Helmi Zulhaidi Mohd Shafri|Abdallah Shanableh|Rami Al-Ruzouq|Aimrun Wayayok|Shaiful Jahari bin Hashim|Mourtadha Sarhan Sachit
limitations: Authors acknowledge several limitations: (1) Manual delineation of date palm leaves is challenging - some leaf ends were unintentionally ignored during ground truth preparation, causing models to miss portions of leaves in predictions; (2) Circular crown delineation approach may not capture full extent of pinnate leaves; (3) Higher computational cost and training time for Swin Transformers (35.7h for Swin-Small vs 13.6h for ResNet-50-FPN); (4) Slower inference speed for Swin models (~0.11-0.137 fps) limits real-time applications; (5) Cross-environment testing limited to same biome/region (UAE agroforestry) - no evaluation across different biomes (tropical, temperate forests); (6) Performance degrades significantly at coarse resolutions (>20cm GSD); (7) Fixed CNN receptive fields limit long-range dependency modeling; (8) Requires large labeled dataset (89,069 images) for training; (9) Manual annotation effort is substantial for large-scale applications.

title: Zero-Shot Tree Detection and Segmentation from Aerial Forest Imagery
authors: Michelle Chen|David Russell|Amritha Pallavoor|Derek Young|Jane Wu
venue: ICLR 2025 Machine Learning for Remote Sensing (ML4RS) Workshop
limitations: Authors acknowledge that SAM2 tends to over-segment in the absence of meaningful prompts because it does not distinguish between object classes, resulting in low precision scores. The model requires either careful prompting or post-processing to achieve tree-specific segmentation. While recall is comparable to specialized models, precision remains a challenge in pure zero-shot mode. More extensive quantitative evaluations are needed beyond the benchmark datasets tested. The paper notes that while SAM2 shows promise, it is not technically an object detection model, so direct comparison with detection models has limitations.

title: Semantic-Aware Cross-Modal Transfer for UAV-LiDAR Individual Tree Segmentation
authors: Fuyang Zhou|Haiqing He|Ting Chen|Tao Zhang|Minglu Yang|Ye Yuan|Jiahao Liu
limitations: Authors acknowledge several limitations: (1) MSFFNet struggles to extract some smaller tree crowns, particularly in dense canopy scenarios with crown overlap, texture similarity among tree species, and varying forest types; (2) The method does not handle understory tree segmentation—a persistent challenge for 2D image-based forest surveys; (3) Segmentation accuracy depends on registration precision between MPC and LiDAR point clouds; while end-to-end deep learning could avoid this dependency, it would incur much higher computational costs and require large annotated forest point cloud datasets, which are currently scarce; (4) Unifying coordinate systems in scenarios with diverse sensor types and point cloud generation methods remains an open research topic; (5) The method has not been tested in deciduous or tropical broadleaf forests with seasonal foliage variation; (6) Runtime of approximately 190 minutes for 3.2 million points indicates computational cost, though this scales linearly with area and code is not optimized for minimal runtime.

title: REO-VLM: Transforming VLM to Meet Regression Challenges in Earth Observation
authors: Xizhe Xue|Guoting Wei|Hao Chen|Haokui Zhang|Feng Lin|Chunhua Shen|Xiao Xiang Zhu
limitations: Authors acknowledge multiple limitations: (1) Relatively small image patch sizes (250m×250m) limit spatial detail capture and ability to represent complex environmental patterns; (2) Performance gap vs specialist models (REO-VLM 75.59 RMSE vs Niconet 69.0 RMSE for AGB regression); (3) Fundamental challenge in treating numeric regression as token-based text generation - cross-entropy optimization struggles with accurate numeric prediction (evidenced by negative R² for ecological patch counting); (4) RGB-based bridging strategy for heterogeneous modalities (MS, SAR) cannot fully exploit unique characteristics of each sensor despite retaining essential information; (5) Long-tail distribution of AGB values makes large value prediction challenging; (6) Dropout operation incompatible with regression tasks due to variance shift between training and test; (7) Excessive visual information (all layers) disrupts optimization; (8) Model requires large-scale labeled dataset (1.6M pairs) for training.

title: Large-Scale Date Palm Tree Segmentation from Multiscale UAV-Based and Aerial Images Using Deep Vision Transformers
authors: Mohamed Barakat A. Gibril|Helmi Zulhaidi Mohd Shafri|Rami Al-Ruzouq|Abdallah Shanableh|Faten Nahas|Saeed Al Mansoori
limitations: Authors acknowledge: (1) Manual ground-truth preparation via visual assessment may create boundaries slightly larger or smaller than actual tree crowns, potentially decreasing accuracy metrics; (2) Limited spectral information of RGB images poses challenges; (3) High intraclass variance of date palm trees (cultivar, age, crown size, height) complicates segmentation; (4) Variations in spatial resolutions across multisource data; (5) Complexity of image backgrounds and contexts; (6) UperNet-Swin model has high computational cost despite excellent performance; (7) Performance degrades significantly (11-23.5%) when spatial resolution decreases from 5cm to 20cm GSD; (8) Substantial performance drop beyond 20cm GSD (to 62-68% at 25-30cm).

title: TreeSeg—A Toolbox for Fully Automated Tree Crown Segmentation Based on High-Resolution Multispectral UAV Data
authors: Sönke Speckenwirth|Melanie Brandmeier|Sebastian Paczkowski
limitations: Authors acknowledge several key limitations: (1) Predicted masks lack the level of detail present in ground truth labels with refined branch-level edges, 'which might be due to the small amount of training data' (800 trees). (2) IoU of 65% means 35% of assigned pixels contain false information that could 'distort further data analysis, e.g., crown vitality assessment.' Authors emphasize widely accepted 50% IoU threshold is 'insufficient for further purpose-driven analysis.' (3) SAM shows 'such poor results' (21% IoU) that it is not recommended for use despite being included for transparency. (4) Image enhancement causes boundary blurring between trees and background, reducing shape precision despite improving IoU. (5) Model trained on single forest type (temperate mixed forest in Germany), so 'comparability to other results is limited since these studies focus on different types of forests.' (6) Small dataset size limits model's ability to learn fine details: 'most studies use coarser labels for tree crown segmentation, achieving better results in terms of accuracy metrics, but not in terms of the required level of detail.' (7) SAM inference time 'may take more than a day depending on hardware resources' making it impractical. (8) Authors note need for 'larger and more diverse dataset' to enable generalization across different forest types and ecosystems.

title: Tree Species Classification from UAV Canopy Images with Deep Learning Models
authors: Yunmei Huang|Botong Ou|Kexin Meng|Baijian Yang|Joshua Carpenter|Jinha Jung|Songlin Fei
limitations: The study's limitations include an imbalanced number of images among species, a focus on plantation forests which may limit generalizability to natural forests, and variations in Ground Sampling Distance (GSD) that could introduce uncertainty. The authors also highlight the lack of an open-source benchmark dataset for this task as a broader challenge.

title: Assessing SAM for Tree Crown Instance Segmentation from Drone Imagery
authors: Mélisande Teng|Arthur Ouaknine|Etienne Laliberté|Yoshua Bengio|David Rolnick|Hugo Larochelle
venue: ICLR 2025 Machine Learning for Remote Sensing (ML4RS) Workshop
limitations: Authors acknowledge: (1) SAM out-of-the-box is inadequate despite being presented as user-friendly tool - requires task-specific tuning; (2) High-resolution imagery and photogrammetry artifacts cause SAM to focus on irrelevant details when used with CNN prompts; (3) Study limited to single region (Quebec) - generalization to other biomes/regions not tested; (4) Performance varies significantly by species abundance, with rare species showing lower accuracy; (5) DSMPrompter's advantage over RSPrompter is modest, suggesting limits to DSM integration benefits; (6) Computational requirements of SAM (ViT-H) not fully characterized for operational deployment. Future work identified: studying different DSM integration methods, assessing effect of resolution degradation, determining if DSMPrompter advantages increase in low-data regimes.

title: Tree Species Classification in UAV Remote Sensing Images Based on Super-Resolution Reconstruction and Deep Learning
authors: Yingkang Huang|Xiaorong Wen|Yuanyun Gao|Yanli Zhang|Guozhong Lin
limitations: Authors acknowledge: (1) Limited spatial resolution of low-altitude aerial images introduces degradation (detail loss, brightness reduction, blurred edges, weak texture) affecting CNN feature extraction; (2) Real-ESRGAN super-resolution technique has limitations and could be improved with more fuzzy kernels and enhanced algorithms; (3) Small inter-class differences and significant intra-class differences among tree species due to forest canopy closure, lighting, background, and shooting height variations; (4) Hardware limitations of drone imaging equipment cause blurred tree crown boundaries and weak texture factors; (5) Canopy images differ from natural images—mutual relationships between tree canopies affect classification in medium-to-high density forests; (6) Intra-canopy heterogeneity at individual tree level but repeated similarity at overall level; (7) Study limited to single location (Dongtai Forest Farm) with no cross-site validation; (8) Dataset relatively modest in scale (4,338 samples) compared to general computer vision benchmarks.

title: A DISTRIBUTION SHIFT BENCHMARK FOR SMALLHOLDER AGROFORESTRY: DO FOUNDATION MODELS IMPROVE GEOGRAPHIC GENERALIZATION?
authors: Siddharth Sachdeva|Isabel Lopez|Chandrashekhar Biradar|David Lobell
venue: ICLR 2024 Machine Learning for Remote Sensing (ML4RS) Workshop
limitations: High overall accuracy from traditional cross-validation can hide poor generalization and wide variations in accuracy across different regions. A significant generalization gap persists even with advanced foundation models, suggesting that a data-centric approach focusing on geographically stratified ground-truth data collection is a more practical solution until foundation models are trained on more diverse remote sensing data.

title: TiMo: Spatiotemporal Foundation Model for Satellite Image Time Series
authors: Xiaolei Qin|Di Wang|Jing Zhang|Fengxiang Wang|Xin Su|Bo Du|Liangpei Zhang
limitations: 1) Geographic bias in MillionST: 'images mainly collected from Europe, North Africa, and West Asia, it cannot represent the larger set', limiting global generalization claims; 2) Computational cost: 'Computational cost remains barrier for real-time/on-device deployment' despite D-STGA efficiency improvements; 3) GPU memory requirements: M-M-M-M configuration causes Out-of-Memory on RTX 4090; Practical configurations require 14-15GB memory; 4) 'STGA computational cost increases rapidly with temporal length T' before D-STGA optimization (O(T²) → O(T)); 5) Temporal length constraint: 'Limited GPU memory only supports simultaneous processing of images with temporal length of 3' during experiments despite MillionST having 10 phases; 6) Pre-training resource intensity: Requires 100 epochs on large-scale dataset with multiple high-end GPUs; 7) Cross-sensor transfer challenging: 'Challenging transfer from optical to SAR images' noted for KuroSiwo; 8) Mask unit design: 1×32×32 mask unit may not be optimal for all SITS characteristics or temporal intervals.

title: Large-scale assessment of date palm plantations based on UAV remote sensing and multiscale vision transformer
authors: Mohamed Barakat A. Gibril|Helmi Zulhaidi Mohd Shafri|Abdallah Shanableh|Rami Al-Ruzouq|Shaiful Jahari bin Hashim|Aimrun Wayayok|Mourtadha Sarhan Sachit
venue: Remote Sensing Applications: Society and Environment
limitations: Model requires high-resolution data (<0.5m GSD) for accurate detection, with significant performance degradation beyond this threshold. Visual evaluation criteria for health assessment introduce subjectivity due to personal interpretations. Limited class variations in training dataset and vast diversity of palm trees present challenges for species differentiation. Specific intricate scenarios (delicate green canopy, dense crown mixed with grey areas) present classification challenges. To refine health assessment capabilities and extend functionality to identify RPW infestation stages, a thorough ground-truth dataset encompassing diverse infestation stages is essential, requiring multidisciplinary collaboration with date palm experts. The approach currently provides generic indicators of healthy/unhealthy trees but requires further development for detailed pest and disease diagnosis.

title: Application of the Vision Transformer and Mask R-CNN Joint Algorithm to Assist Forest Decisions
authors: Qinrui Liang
venue: 2023 5th International Conference on Geoscience and Remote Sensing Mapping (GRSM)
limitations: Authors identify multiple limitations: 1) ViT performs mediocrely on small-to-moderate datasets (67% accuracy) and requires extensive training time and data volume for high-resolution imagery; 2) Appropriate parameter settings (patch size, learning rate, etc.) are critical but require extensive tuning; 3) Mask R-CNN requires high-quality manual annotations which are time-consuming, and struggles with dense plant growth and small/young trees where instance segmentation fails; 4) Forest feature similarity makes classification challenging without fine-grained crown segmentation; 5) High computational requirements limit training duration; 6) Temporal and geographic errors can occur from delayed aerial photography; 7) High-resolution monitoring infrastructure (AOP with LiDAR and imaging spectrometers) involves substantial costs and deployment risks; 8) Image preprocessing (resizing, cutting) required for model compatibility reduces data accuracy.

title: e-TransUNet: TransUNet provides a strong spatial transformation for precise deforestation mapping
authors: Ali Jamali|Swalpa Kumar Roy|Biswajeet Pradhan
venue: Remote Sensing Applications: Society and Environment
limitations: Authors acknowledge that e-TransUNet entails slightly increased time complexity compared to base TransUNet due to utilization of attention gates and spatial transformation mechanisms. While Vision Transformers (ViTs) have demonstrated superior performance compared to CNNs, they face challenges including computational complexity (increasing processing costs) and requirement for more labeled input data compared to CNNs. The paper addresses some but not all of these challenges.

title: 3D LiDAR Transformer for City-scale Vegetation Segmentation and Biomass Estimation
authors: Asim Khan|Warda Asim|Muhammad Ibrahim|Anwaar Ulhaq
venue: 2022 International Conference on Digital Image Computing: Techniques and Applications (DICTA)
limitations: Authors acknowledge that current methods for large-scale 3D LiDAR data analysis for ecological observations remain challenging. They note that conventional remotely sensing systems using passive optical sensors have limitations in providing accurate horizontal and vertical dimensional data, which motivated their LiDAR-based approach. The paper mentions that 'accurate semantic segmentation of 3D point clouds has been a long-time problem' due to the 'unstructured nature of point clouds' which makes it 'difficult to develop deep neural architectures.' They also note challenges including point cloud data overlap, varying sample density, and lack of clear structure.

title: M2fNet: Multi-modal Forest Monitoring Network on Large-scale Virtual Dataset
authors: Yawen Lu|Yunhan Huang|Su Sun|Tansi Zhang|Xuewen Zhang|Songlin Fei|Victor Chen
venue: IEEE Conference on Virtual Reality and 3D User Interfaces Abstracts and Workshops (VRW)
limitations: Authors acknowledge several limitations: (1) Virtual datasets may not accurately represent diversity of real forests in species composition and ecosystem variability, potentially leading to biased decision-making; (2) Method assumes RGB or RGB+depth modalities and may not extend to other modalities like text; (3) Model trained on forest scenes shows large performance gap when applied to specific outdoor environments like streets or indoor environments; (4) Virtual dataset approach may inadvertently neglect social aspects of forest management such as impacts on local communities and indigenous knowledge; (5) Specific environments with visual appearance substantially different from training focus do not perform well.

title: Fine-tuning of Geospatial Foundation Models for Aboveground Biomass Estimation
authors: Michal Muszynski|Levente Klein|Ademir Ferreira da Silva|Anjani Prasad Atluri|Carlos Gomes|Daniela Szwarcman|Gurkanwar Singh|Kewen Gu|Maciel Zortea|Naomi Simumba|Paolo Fraccaro|Shraddha Singh|Steve Meliksetian|Campbell Watson|Daiki Kimura|Harini Srinivasan
limitations: Authors acknowledge that U-Net slightly outperforms GFMs in overall RMSE. Future work needed to integrate new multimodal data sources (e.g., radar for persistent cloud cover) and test models under more realistic conditions. The preprocessing methodology requires excluding cloud-contaminated images. Space-based LiDAR measurements (GEDI, ICESat-2) are sparse in spatial distribution, requiring geostatistical methods to transform into spatially continuous AGB estimates. Label-limited problems are common in forest-based applications.

title: Classification of Individual Tree Species Using UAV LiDAR Based on Transformer
authors: Peng Sun|Xuguang Yuan|Dan Li
limitations: Authors acknowledge several limitations: (1) Dense canopy overlap in Quercus mongolica forests limits LiDAR penetration, resulting in sparse trunk information and lower classification accuracy; (2) Study conducted in artificial forest with flat terrain and patterned distribution (easier than natural forests); (3) Excessive point density (>4096) introduces redundant information causing slower convergence and potential accuracy reduction; (4) Method requires relatively high-resolution LiDAR data (1772 points/m²); (5) Morphological similarity between broad-leaved species (Quercus mongolica and Birch) makes classification more challenging compared to distinguishing coniferous from broad-leaved trees; (6) Need for future work combining multi-source LiDAR technology for more complex natural forest situations.

title: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning of Vision Foundation Model for Forest Floor Segmentation from UAV Imagery
authors: Mohammad Wasil|Ahmad Drak|Brennan Penfold|Ludovico Scarton|Maximilian Johenneken|Alexander Asteroth|Sebastian Houben
venue: IEEE ICRA Workshop - Novel Approaches for Precision Agriculture and Forestry with Autonomous Robots
limitations: Labeling inconsistencies in the Garrulus dataset contribute to performance issues, particularly in the CWD class where many instances are incorrectly labeled or entirely missed. The subjective nature of object definitions (e.g., what constitutes CWD) leads to confusion—upside-down logs labeled as CWD share visual similarities with STUMP class, causing prediction errors. Recall performance consistently lower than precision due to these annotation issues. Zero-shot SAM struggles with vegetation segmentation where boundaries lack clear separation from background. The model shows lower per-class mIoU for MISC and STUMP classes. Future work needed includes: on-the-fly adaptation to different locations and environmental conditions, exploring real-time distillation of foundation models, investigating feasibility of online training directly on UAV platforms, and integrating obstacle-free area identification into seeding pipeline.

title: TreeFormer: a Semi-Supervised Transformer-based Framework for Tree Counting from a Single High Resolution Image
authors: Hamed Amini Amirkolaee|Miaojing Shi|Mark Mulligan
limitations: Authors acknowledge: (1) Counting trees in dense canopy where trees are interlocking in continuous form is very complex, (2) The model's generalizability on heterogeneous datasets (e.g., NEON dataset) across different domains requires domain generalization and adaptation techniques as future work, (3) Performance depends on background complexity - complex urban scenes with buildings, cars, and varied vegetation are more challenging than simple tree-grass contrast, (4) Lower spatial resolution degrades accuracy, (5) Trees with different types, sizes, shapes, and densities present varying difficulty levels, (6) Annotation burden remains substantial even with semi-supervised approach - creating manual point annotations for 95,067 trees is time-consuming

title: Individual Tree Detection Based on High-Resolution RGB Images for Urban Forestry Applications
authors: Lishuo Zhang|Hong Lin|Feng Wang
limitations: Method is not effective enough to handle intersection and agglomeration of trees - overlapping trees detected as single tree. Performance degrades in dense forests where many trees overlap with each other. Detection of high-density objects remains challenging, consistent with other methods in the field. Missed detections occur in areas of agglomeration. The method occasionally produces false detections (16 FP in street tree test), though significantly fewer than ResNet50 baseline (33 FP). Manual labeling is time consuming and labor intensive, motivating the semi-supervised approach. Initial model without fine-tuning showed poor performance on new datasets with low confidence scores.

title: Expanding Vision in Tree Counting: Novel Ground Truth Generation and Deep Learning Model
authors: Minh Nhat Ton-That|Tin Viet Le|Nhien Hao Truong|An Dinh Le|Anh-Duy Pham|Hien Bich Vo
venue: 2024 Tenth International Conference on Communications and Electronics (ICCE)
limitations: Authors acknowledge multiple limitations: (1) Computational constraints limited experiments to 1536×1536 images, though larger images may further improve performance; (2) Ground truth generation time scales poorly with image size (10 hours for 1536×1536 vs 2 hours for 512×512); (3) Future work needed to explore correlation between image size and model quality systematically; (4) Computational cost considerations remain for practical deployment; (5) Batch size of 1 introduces training noise, though transformers are more robust to this than CNNs; (6) No systematic exploration of optimal image size for ground truth generation performed.

title: MTCDNet: Multimodal Feature Fusion-Based Tree Crown Detection Network Using UAV-Acquired Optical Imagery and LiDAR Data
authors: Heng Zhang|Can Yang|Xijian Fan
limitations: Authors acknowledge: (1) Model fails to detect small-sized tree crowns in densely populated regions due to close spatial proximity and blurred texture/edge information; (2) Struggles with detecting large-sized tree crowns with significant scale variation or irregular contours; (3) Multi-scale ability needs improvement for handling densely packed small objects and singular large targets; (4) Higher computational overhead (especially with 8 attention heads: 45.31 GFLOPs) poses challenges for real-time deployment on resource-constrained UAV platforms; (5) More attention heads may increase overfitting risk when training dataset is limited; (6) Performance degradation under stricter AP75 metric in dense forests where crown overlap makes boundary delineation challenging

title: BARE: Boundary-Aware with Resolution Enhancement for Tree Crown Delineation
authors: Attavit Wilaiwongsakul|Bin Liang|Wenfeng Jia|Bryan Zheng|Fang Chen
limitations: Authors acknowledge multiple limitations: (1) Evaluation uses only OAM-TCD dataset; generalizability across other remote sensing domains requires validation; (2) Study examines only three architectural paradigms (SegFormer, PSPNet, SETR); effectiveness on newer transformers like Swin remains unexplored; (3) Only bilinear upsampling employed; learned upsampling may yield different results; (4) Memory constraints necessitated different gradient accumulation strategies across architectures; (5) Deeper analysis of mechanisms driving architecture-specific responses to combined training strategies would strengthen understanding.
